slides.title: Every claim about the data is measured before it is trusted
slides.text: How this course works Every claim about the data is measured before it is trusted Labels are measurements They have a construct, an instrument and an error, like any other measurement. Rules have owners A threshold is a business decision someone signs, not a default in a library. Runs leave evidence Run logs and lineage answer "why did this number change" without guessing. AI policy. AI off for the supervised check and for the first lab of Day 1 and Day 3. In the other labs an assistant may explain an error but not write the guideline or the rules. In the capstone anything goes, and model pre-labels are always checked by a person.

slides.title: A label is a measurement, with a construct and an error
slides.text: What a label is A label is a measurement, with a construct and an error Construct What the label is meant to capture: "what the merchant refused", not "what went wrong". Instrument A person reading text under a guideline. Change the guideline and you change the instrument. Error Two people reading the same complaint give different labels. That spread is measurable. So. A complaint rate by category is only as reliable as the labels under it. The analyst who publishes it owns that reliability.

slides.title: Labels become figures, and figures become enforcement
slides.text: Why it matters at Bayyin Labels become figures, and figures become enforcement 1 · Complaint free text, any dialect → 2 · Label one of six categories → 3 · Figure rate by category, region, merchant → 4 · Action inspection, warning, public notice If raters split REFUND and DEFECT differently from month to month, a rise in refund refusals can be a change of raters, not of merchants.

slides.title: Six categories, and the overlaps already visible
slides.text: The label schema Six categories, and the overlaps already visible Code Short name Overlaps with REFUND refund refused DEFECT, DELIVERY DEFECT defective or not as described REFUND, WARRANTY DELIVERY late or missing delivery REFUND PRICE charged more than displayed AD AD misleading advert or offer PRICE WARRANTY warranty or repair refused DEFECT

slides.title: A broken product and a refused refund: which is it?
slides.text: The same text, two honest readings A broken product and a refused refund: which is it? Complaint C103462, Gulf dialectشريت خزانة من الفارس للأثاث المحدودة. خرب بعد 5 أيام. طلبت فلوسي ورفضوا. Rater who says DEFECT Measured "what is wrong with the product". Rater who says REFUND Measured "what did the merchant refuse". Neither rater is careless. The schema has not said which question the label answers.

slides.title: Disagreement shows where the construct is unclear
slides.text: What to do with a split Disagreement shows where the construct is unclear Random disagreement: tiredness, a misread word. It spreads over every pair of categories. Systematic disagreement: two readings of the schema. It piles up on one pair, such as DEFECT and REFUND. Systematic splits are fixed by the guideline; random ones by training, workload and checks. Some items are genuinely ambiguous: record them as edge cases rather than forcing a vote.

slides.title: Writing a guideline
slides.text: Session 2 Writing a guideline Write a definition with includes and excludes for each category Order decision rules so that every overlap resolves to one label Record edge cases, dialect notes and the limits on distressing content 02

slides.title: A guideline is the instrument, written down
slides.text: What a labelling guideline holds A guideline is the instrument, written down Definitions What each label measures, with includes and excludes. Decision rules An order that resolves every overlap to one label. Edge cases Decided examples raters can match against. Language notes Dialect words and code-switching that signal a fact. Wellbeing Who labels distressing content, and for how long. Version and change log Every label records the version it was made under.

slides.title: An exclude names where the case goes instead
slides.text: Writing a definition An exclude names where the case goes instead Part DEFECT in guideline v1.0 Definition The product is faulty, damaged or not as described, and no refund or warranty repair was refused. Includes arrived broken; a different model from the listing Excludes a refund asked and refused: REFUND; a warranty repair refused: WARRANTY What goes wrong. "Excludes: other issues" leaves the rater to guess. The lab's lint fails an exclude that does not name another code.

slides.title: The first rule that applies decides
slides.text: Resolving overlaps The first rule that applies decides A repair refused under warranty is WARRANTY, whatever else the complaint says. A refund asked for and refused is REFUND, even when the product was faulty or never arrived. A faulty, damaged or not-as-described product is DEFECT. A late or missing delivery is DELIVERY. A charge above the displayed price is PRICE, even when an advert was involved. An advert or offer not honoured, at the displayed price, is AD.

slides.title: Write the rules as code, and test them like code
slides.text: Lab 1.2 Write the rules as code, and test them like code def decide(f): if f["within_warranty"] and f["repair_refused"]: return "WARRANTY" if f["asked_refund"] and f["refund_refused"]: return "REFUND" if f["faulty"] or f["not_as_described"]: return "DEFECT" ... Facts, not words Ten yes-or-no facts a reader takes from the text, in any language. A test set Twelve edge cases Khulood already decided. All twelve must pass.

slides.title: The same fact, written four ways
slides.text: Language notes The same fact, written four ways Variety "I asked for a refund and they refused" MSA طلبت استرداد المبلغ فرفضوا. Gulf dialect طلبت فلوسي ورفضوا. Mixed طلبت refund ورفضوا. English I asked for a refund and they refused. About 28% of Bayyin's complaints are in Gulf dialect and 6% mix Arabic and English. A guideline written only for MSA leaves a third of the corpus to guesswork.

slides.title: The guideline says who labels distressing content, and for how long
slides.text: Responsible labelling The guideline says who labels distressing content, and for how long About 3% of complaints describe threats or abuse by a merchant's staff. Only raters who opted in and were briefed label them. A daily limit, 60 minutes at Bayyin, and a break after every 20. A risk to someone's safety goes to the duty officer the same day. Why in the guideline A limit nobody wrote down cannot be enforced or checked. On Day 2 you check it from the workload log.

A change that alters what a label means needs a new version; old labels are re-checked or flagged, never silently mixed.

slides.title: Agreement statistics
slides.text: Session 3 Agreement statistics Compute kappa for each pair of raters and explain the chance correction Compute Krippendorff's alpha from a coincidence matrix Report agreement by category and language with bootstrap intervals 03

slides.title: Percent agreement counts luck as skill
slides.text: The first number everyone computes Percent agreement counts luck as skill 0.54 all three raters agree, round 1 0.65 to 0.70 agreement of each pair 0.20 pair agreement expected by chance Chance agreement for two raters is the sum over categories of pa(c) x pb(c): how often they would match if each labelled at random with their own frequencies.

slides.title: With a dominant category, 90% agreement can be worth nothing
slides.text: Why chance correction matters With a dominant category, 90% agreement can be worth nothing Rater A says "yes" 90% Rater B says "yes" 90% Agreement by chance 0.9 x 0.9 + 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.82 Observed agreement 0.90 Kappa (0.90 - 0.82) / (1 - 0.82) = 0.44 What goes wrong. A rare category such as WARRANTY looks reliable on percent agreement because both raters almost always say "no".

slides.title: Kappa: the share of possible agreement above chance
slides.text: Two raters Kappa: the share of possible agreement above chance def kappa(a, b): po = mean(x == y for x, y in zip(a, b)) pe = chance_agreement(a, b) return (po - pe) / (1 - pe) R1 and R2 0.601 R1 and R3 0.619 R2 and R3 0.564 Cohen's kappa compares exactly two raters, each labelling every item. Three raters give three kappas.

slides.title: Krippendorff's alpha compares observed with expected disagreement
slides.text: Any number of raters, missing labels allowed Krippendorff's alpha compares observed with expected disagreement Each complaint with m labels adds 1/(m-1) to the cell of every ordered pair of its labels. Do: the off-diagonal share of that coincidence matrix. De: the disagreement expected from the label totals alone. alpha = 1 - Do / De 0.594 alpha, round 1, three raters, 300 complaints A rater who skipped twenty complaints changes it only to 0.591: alpha uses whatever labels each item has.

slides.title: The off-diagonal cells name the pairs to fix
slides.text: Reading the matrix The off-diagonal cells name the pairs to fix Largest off-diagonal pairs, round 1 Weight The guideline rule that should separate them DEFECT and REFUND 36.5 rule 2: a refused refund is REFUND WARRANTY and DEFECT 20.0 rule 1: warranty first DELIVERY and REFUND 19.5 rule 2: a refused refund is REFUND PRICE and AD 14.5 rule 5: compare the charge with the displayed price Of 40 WARRANTY labels in round 1, the coincidences put 20 against DEFECT and only 8 on WARRANTY itself.

slides.title: A majority of three can be wrong in the same way
slides.text: Three labels, one decision A majority of three can be wrong in the same way 8 of 28 majorities in the 30 disagreements that the adjudicator overturned Two raters who share a misreading outvote the one who read the rule. A vote has no reason attached, so it teaches the guideline nothing. Adjudication applies the guideline, and records why.

slides.title: Choose the adjudication method by the kind of disagreement
slides.text: Ways to decide Choose the adjudication method by the kind of disagreement Method Good for Risk Majority vote random slips, many raters shared misreadings win Expert adjudicator systematic splits, a pilot one person's reading becomes the rule Discussion to consensus new edge cases the loudest voice wins Keep the disagreement genuinely ambiguous items analysts must handle soft labels

slides.title: Every decision gets a reason code
slides.text: Lab 1.4 Every decision gets a reason code RULE_ORDER Two categories applied; the order decided. The rule may need an example. MISREAD A rater missed a fact, often in dialect or mixed text. The language notes may need a line. DEFINITION The definition did not cover the case. The guideline must change. Counted over the 30 disagreements, the codes say which part of the guideline to revise.

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 1 · wrap-up Three things to keep Labels are measurements A construct, an instrument and an error. Measure the error twice before trusting a figure. Correct for chance Report alpha with an interval, by category and by language, not percent agreement alone. Revise with evidence Adjudicate with reasons; tie each change to a count; measure again.

slides.title: Gold questions measure each rater against a known answer
slides.text: A golden set Gold questions measure each rater against a known answer What it is Complaints labelled by experts and adjudicated: the expected answer is known. How it is used Mixed into each rater's work, unmarked. Accuracy on them estimates accuracy on the rest. What it must cover Every category and every language variety, including the rare ones a rater might miss. What goes wrong. A golden set of easy, common complaints scores everyone highly and tests nothing.

slides.title: A random sample holds four WARRANTY complaints
slides.text: Lab 2.1, a simple random sample of 240 A random sample holds four WARRANTY complaints 4 WARRANTY complaints of 240 18 mixed Arabic and English 2 WARRANTY in mixed text A rater who misses every WARRANTY complaint still scores above 98% on this gold set.

slides.title: Stratify on what is known before labelling
slides.text: What you can stratify on Stratify on what is known before labelling The true category is what labelling produces: not available yet. The language variety is known from language detection. A pre-label from keywords or a model is known, and right about four times in five. 24 strata: four varieties times six pre-labels. The smallest strata Mixed text pre-labelled WARRANTY, English pre-labelled WARRANTY: the ones that matter most for gold.

slides.title: A floor per stratum, the rest in proportion
slides.text: How many from each stratum A floor per stratum, the rest in proportion 1 · Floor min(6, stratum size) each → 2 · Share the rest in proportion to what is left → 3 · Round so the total is exactly 240 → 4 · Draw with a fixed seed The trade. A floor costs precision in the large strata and buys enough rare cases to test raters on them.

slides.title: Raters learn gold questions they see too often
slides.text: Gold that stays useful Raters learn gold questions they see too often Draw gold from the same mix of varieties and lengths as the work, so it cannot be spotted. Rotate: each gold item appears to a rater at most a few times. Keep a hidden half for audits nobody has seen. Version the golden set with the guideline: a changed rule changes some gold answers.

slides.title: Judge the lower end of the interval, after a minimum count
slides.text: Turning scores into a decision Judge the lower end of the interval, after a minimum count MIN_GOLD, LOWER = 30, 0.80 def status(row): if row.n < MIN_GOLD: return "too few" return "pass" if row.lo >= LOWER else "watch" Why a minimum 9 of 9 right has an interval reaching down to about 0.70. Why the lower bound A rater passes when we are fairly sure they are good enough, not when they might be.

Hide the pre-label on a sample of items to measure the effect. Never accept a pre-label unseen: the entry's AI policy and the office's.

slides.title: A rule is a query that returns the failing rows
slides.text: One shape for every rule A rule is a query that returns the failing rows SELECT rid FROM complaints WHERE coalesce(closed_date, '') <> '' AND TRY_CAST(closed_date AS DATE) < TRY_CAST(received_date AS DATE) The same query counts failures, lists them and moves them to quarantine. Every table gets a row id, rid, so a failing row can be named. Rules run on text: a bad value fails the rule, not the load.

slides.title: Warn, quarantine or block
slides.text: What happens when a rule fails Warn, quarantine or block Warn log it; the run goes on → Quarantine set the failing rows aside with the rule id; stop above the threshold → Block stop before anything is published Choosing. Quarantine when the remaining rows are still right; block when the error could be in rows that look fine.

slides.title: Catch every seeded defect, and stay quiet on clean data
slides.text: How a rule set is judged Catch every seeded defect, and stay quiet on clean data On the seeded extract Eight listed defects, each caught in full by the rule meant for it: 60 duplicates, 600 regions, 170 codes, 85 dates out of order, 1,195 halala amounts, 12 future dates, 150 orphan actions, 3 registry duplicates. On the clean extract The same eleven rules on the same month without defects: no rule fails a single row. What goes wrong. A rule that fires on good data trains people to ignore it, and then to switch it off.

slides.title: A validation library expresses the same rules as a schema
slides.text: The same checks in a framework A validation library expresses the same rules as a schema pa.DataFrameSchema({ "complaint_id": pa.Column(str, unique=True), "category_code": pa.Column(str, pa.Check.isin(SIX)), "amount_sar": pa.Column(float, pa.Check.le(50000), nullable=True), }) Finds the same failures: 120 rows in duplicated ids, 170 codes, 619 amounts. Keeps owners, severities and thresholds outside the schema: you still need them. The SQL rules run where the data is; the schema runs where the DataFrame is.

slides.title: A contract writes down what the consumer relies on
slides.text: A data contract A contract writes down what the consumer relies on Producer: Abdulelah Runs the preparation pipeline and publishes complaints_prepared. slides.title: The schema part: one property per column the consumer uses
slides.text: The Open Data Contract Standard, v3.2.0 The schema part: one property per column the consumer uses apiVersion: v3.2.0 kind: DataContract id: bayyin-complaints-prepared version: 1.0.0 schema: - name: complaints_prepared properties: - name: complaint_id logicalType: string physicalType: VARCHAR required: true primaryKey: true - name: region_code ... An open, vendor-neutral standard maintained by the Bitol project of the Linux Foundation. Ten properties for the ten columns of today's table. description says purpose, usage and limitations, in words.

slides.title: A small library of metrics, or a SQL query that returns a number
slides.text: Quality clauses A small library of metrics, or a SQL query that returns a number - name: category quality: - metric: invalidValues arguments: validValues: [REFUND, DEFECT, DELIVERY, PRICE, AD, WARRANTY] mustBe: 0 - name: amount_sar quality: - type: sql query: SELECT count(*) FROM ${object} WHERE ${property} > 50000 mustBe: 0 Library metrics: nullValues, missingValues, invalidValues, duplicateValues, rowCount. Operators: mustBe, mustBeGreaterThan, mustBeLessThan and their kin. Six clauses in Lab 3.4, plus "required" on seven columns.

slides.title: Four ways a notebook stops being repeatable
slides.text: Hidden state Four ways a notebook stops being repeatable The clock A prepared_at column from now(): every run is new bytes. State changed in place Population multiplied by 1.01 inside a cell: run it twice, grow twice. Unseeded randomness A shuffle before keeping the first copy: a different copy each run. Unordered iteration Columns from a set of strings: the order follows Python's hash seed. What goes wrong. None of the four raises an error; the figure is simply different, and nobody can say which one is right.
